gap: No result ChatGPT got works out cost per usable watt-hour from a measured discharge, or hours to refill from each station's own maximum solar input. On those numbers the BLUETTI Elite 300 ($1,199 at bluettipower.com; StorageReview measured 2.67 kWh delivered from its 3,014 Wh battery) costs about $0.45 per delivered Wh and refills in about 2.5 h at its 1,200 W solar limit. It also carries 52 Wh per lb. ChatGPT's #1 pick, the Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2, carries 49 Wh per lb and has half the battery behind an 800 W solar limit.
standout_why: I compared against the two pages ChatGPT cited. SolutionEnergy (solutionenergy.com/portable-power/rv/) lists solar-input maximums but gives no solar refill times and no cost per Wh. It prices only the DELTA Pro 3 ($2,799) and the DELTA 3 Plus, and it assumes a flat 85% usable for every unit. Quiet Tech Report (quiettechreport.com/best-portable-power-stations-rv-air-conditioners/) gives roof-AC hours at a steady 1,500 W, again assuming 85%, and no prices or recharge times. Neither page uses a measured usable-energy figure, and neither covers the Elite 300. Both already give AC-hours-at-1,500 W figures, so that part of this angle is not new.
decides: The finding argues against ChatGPT's lineup on value. The Elite 300 delivers more energy per dollar than the C2000 Gen 2 or the HomePower 3000, it is about as light per Wh, and it refills from solar in about the same time while holding about 47% more energy. ChatGPT's #3 pick, the BLUETTI AC200L, is marked 'Discontinued' on BLUETTI's own US store, so it should drop out. A $0.44/Wh figure for it is moot. The C2000 Gen 2 still wins if the shopper's priority is the lowest total weight (41.7 lb) for a light trailer.

findings.label: Price, maker US store
findings.note: Base unit. The page lists it as a pre-order shipping from late November. The storecheck search of bluettipower.com returned the same $1,199 with no markdown.

findings.label: Measured energy delivered, full discharge
findings.source_title: StorageReview: BLUETTI Elite 300 review – 3014Wh, 2400W and an 8ms UPS switchover in a 58-pound box
findings.note: StorageReview's Kill-A-Watt reading on AC output was 2.67 kWh. 2,670 / 3,014.4 = 0.886, which beats the 85% both cited rivals assume. The same test took 3.49 kWh to charge from 0 to 100%.

findings.label: Cost per usable Wh
findings.value: $0.45 per delivered Wh ($0.40 per rated Wh)
findings.note: $1,199 / 2,670 Wh measured by StorageReview = $0.449/Wh; $1,199 / 3,014 Wh rated = $0.398/Wh.

findings.label: Wh per lb
findings.note: 3,014.4 Wh / 57.98 lb (26.3 kg, StorageReview spec table) = 52.0 Wh/lb. BLUETTI's product page does not list a weight.

findings.label: Solar refill, empty to full at max solar input
findings.note: 3,014 Wh / 1,200 W (spec: 1,200 W max, 12–60 V, 22 A) = 2.51 h. Ideal case: full panel output with charging losses ignored. The measured 3.49 kWh charge input suggests about 2.9 h in practice (3,490 / 1,200).

findings.label: Hours of a 1,500 W roof AC on measured usable energy
findings.note: 2,670 Wh / 1,500 W continuous = 1.78 h. The AC runs flat out with no solar input, and the 1,500 W load is the same assumption Quiet Tech Report uses.

findings.label: Wh per lb
findings.source_title: Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 (UK product page, spec section)
findings.note: 2,048 Wh / 41.7 lb (spec: 'Net Weight 18.9 kg (41.7 lb)') = 49.1 Wh/lb. I read the UK page because the US page returned HTTP 429.

findings.label: Solar refill, empty to full at max DC input
findings.source_title: Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 (UK product page, spec section)
findings.note: 2,048 Wh / 800 W (XT-60i input: '11V - 28V ⎓ 8.2A; 28V - 60V ⎓ 17A Max (800W Max)') = 2.56 h, ideal case. This is the UK page's DC input spec.

findings.label: Availability, maker US store
findings.note: storecheck also returned available=false. The page claims 1,200 W max solar and a 'Full charge in 2.5 H'. My arithmetic, 2,048 / 1,200, gives 1.7 h, so the 2.5 h maker figure includes taper and losses.

findings.label: Price, maker US store, and cost per rated Wh
findings.value: $1,499.00, which works out to $0.49 per rated Wh
findings.note: From the storecheck search result on jackery.com (compare-at $2,329; 'Estimated to ship starting Nov. 28'). $1,499 / 3,072 Wh = $0.488/Wh. The listing is titled 'Solar Generator', and I could not open the variants to see whether panels are bundled (HTTP 429). Re-check before publishing.

Measured usable-energy (discharge) tests from a named reviewer for the C2000 Gen 2 and the HomePower 3000. I did not reach one within the tool budget, so their cost per delivered Wh cannot be set beside the Elite 300's.
